learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected 0.75 and locked the reward-gap prediction for a seventy-five-percent pairwise preference under the stated logistic rule.
observations.exploration: At gap zero the predicted preference was fifty percent. Tested 0.75: 67.9%; three: 95.3%; 1.1: 75.0%, a match. Set -1.1: 25.0%, checking the reversal symmetry.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the answer to 1.1, accurately recognized the matched gap and the tested gap three, and explained three-to-one preference odds correspond to log three. It described fitting reward differences from comparison wins rather than receiving explicit scores or reasons.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot at gap 1.1. A purple sigmoid intersected a green dashed seventy-five-percent reference at a highlighted point. Reward-gap and probability axes were distinct, and the matching readout said yes.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884179 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question separates preference probability from a latent score difference.

interaction.reason: Gap changes expose the nonlinear mapping and its reversal.
interaction.evidence: Positive 1.1 gives seventy-five percent while negative 1.1 gives twenty-five.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the fitted difference using odds and the actual trials.
payoff.evidence: It quotes the match and the overconfident gap three.

clarity.reason: The graph and reference line make fitting visible despite technical notation.
clarity.evidence: The observed frequency is a horizontal target rather than the reward-gap axis.

transfer.reason: A real training method is named, but no new comparison set or application is developed.
transfer.evidence: Only one fixed observed preference is fitted.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: A reward number is a fitted gap rather than a directly observed preference score.
surprise.evidence: Seventy-five-percent preference corresponds to about 1.1 under this rule.

visualExplanation.reason: The sigmoid and target line explain why the candidate values differ.
visualExplanation.evidence: The highlighted intersection identifies the correct gap.

playfulness.reason: The slider supports a small fitting puzzle.
playfulness.evidence: Presets and a negative-gap test expose the mapping.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies what a pairwise reward-model target represents.
practicalValue.evidence: The reveal distinguishes comparison outcomes from explicit quality scores or reasons.

depth.reason: The lesson connects probability, odds and a latent difference.
depth.evidence: Log three explains the seventy-five-to-twenty-five odds.

complexity.reason: The controls are easy, but logistic probability, odds and logarithms exceed the everyday learner boundary.
complexity.conceptualDemand: High: infer a latent difference through a nonlinear probability model.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: three presets and one signed slider.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: Reward gaps are transformed parameters, not raw preference percentages.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Reward models, logistic functions, odds and natural logarithms are introduced.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: High: exponential formula, signed gap and logarithm explanation.

whyCool: Human comparison wins can determine a numerical gap even when nobody ever gives a numerical score.
caveat: The toy fixes one answer pair and observed frequency. It does not show multi-pair fitting, uncertainty or general reward-model behavior.
missingEvidence: No fresh preference frequency or multiple-answer fit was tested.
